source.title: Kirby diagrams, trisections and gems of PL 4-manifolds: relationships, results and open problems

accepted.question_text: Does every closed simply-connected 4-manifold admit a trisection in which one of the three 4-dimensional pieces is a 4-disk? Equivalently, is every closed simply-connected 4-manifold decomposable into three 4-dimensional handlebodies whose triple intersection is a closed surface and for which at least one of the 4-dimensional handlebodies has genus 0?

evidence.quote: As a consequence, only simply-connected 4-manifolds can admit trisections where one the 4-dimensional "pieces" is a 4-disk. Viceversa, it is an open problem whether each closed simply-connected 4-manifold admits a trisection with this property, or not: see, for example, [30], [25] and [31].

accepted.question_text: Can one design an algorithm that converts generalized Kirby diagrams with non-orientable 1-handles into gems (5-colored graph encodings of PL 4-manifolds), and can this be done in a way that yields gem-induced trisections for the resulting graphs? If so, this would extend the gem-based estimation of trisection genus from the orientable setting to all closed 4-manifolds, including non-orientable ones.

evidence.quote: As regards Section 3.1, an interesting development would be to obtain an algorithmic procedure to pass from Kirby diagrams to gems in the generalized case of diagrams representing also non-orientable 1-handles (according to [19]). If the resulting gems admitted gem-induced trisections (as happens in the orientable setting: see Theorem 17), in virtue of the non-orientable version of Laudenbach-Poenaru’s result due to [32], an estimation of the trisection genus for all closed 4-manifolds would be obtained, via gems.

accepted.question_text: Given a compact 4-manifold presented only by its 0-, 1-, and 2-handles and a gem of that compact manifold, can one construct a gem of the associated closed 4-manifold even when the original gem contains no ρ_3-pair or ρ_4-pair? More specifically, can one recognize the boundary connected sum #_m(S^1 × S^2) combinatorially and, in useful special cases, find sequences of combinatorial moves that create the ρ_3-pairs needed to pass to a gem of the closed manifold obtained by attaching the 3- and 4-handles?

evidence.quote: Another possible improvement would be to study how to obtain a gem of a closed 4-manifold, starting from a gem of the compact one consisting only of handles up to index two, even if no ρ_3- or ρ_4-pair appears in the latter (as assumed in Proposition 9). The problem is obviously a difficult one, since it involves the combinatorial recognition of #m(S1 ×S2) (m > 0) in 3-dimensional topology, but in specific situations it could possibly be faced, for example by detecting sequences of combinatorial moves yielding the desired ρ_3-pairs.

accepted.question_text: For the double of a compact 4-manifold, a Kirby diagram of the double can be obtained by adding a 0-framed meridian to each framed component of a Kirby diagram of the original manifold. Does the resulting 5-colored graph admit a standard modification procedure that produces ρ_3-pairs satisfying the hypotheses needed to construct a gem of the double?

evidence.quote: A particular case of this problem arises, for instance, in the construction of a gem for the double of a compact 4-manifold. It is known that a Kirby diagram of the double can be obtained, from a Kirby diagram of the manifold itself, by adding a 0-framed meridian to each framed component (see [24]). Therefore, it may be worth investigating whether the particular configuration of the arising 5-colored graph allows to be modified in a standard way so as to give rise to ρ_3-pairs satisfying Proposition 9.

accepted.question_text: Which classes of gems force the trisections obtained from them to realize the actual trisection genus of the represented 4-manifold? This asks for a characterization of 5-colored graph encodings for which the trisection arising either directly as a gem-induced trisection, or indirectly by first taking a compact manifold with connected boundary and then capping off by the canonical 4-dimensional handlebody, is genus-minimizing.

evidence.quote: With respect to Section 3.2, a fundamental problem involves the possible characterization of classes of gems so that the arising trisections (either directly, as gem-induced trisections, or indirectly, via the approach described in Section 3.2.2) realize the trisection genus of the represented 4-manifolds.

accepted.question_text: Which closed simply-connected 4-manifolds admit a gem Γ together with a cyclic ordering ε of the five colors such that the {ε_0,ε_2,ε_4}-colored subgraph and the {ε_1,ε_3,ε_4}-colored subgraph are each connected, and the decomposition T(Γ,ε) is a gem-induced trisection? More broadly, can one characterize topologically the 4-manifolds admitting gems satisfying the hypotheses of Proposition 26, or at least identify substantial classes of manifolds with this property?

evidence.quote: Proposition 26 ([10]) gT (M) = β2(M) for each closed (simply-connected) 4-manifold M which admits a 5-colored graph Γ ∈ G(4)s representing M with gε0,ε2,ε4 = 1 and gε1,ε3,ε4 = 1 (ε being a cyclic permutation of ∆4), so that T (Γ, ε) is a gem-induced trisection.
It would be very interesting to characterize topologically 4-manifolds admitting gems which satisfy the hypotheses of the above statement, or at least to find classes satisfying them.

accepted.question_text: Let M be a compact 4-manifold whose boundary is a connected sum of S^1-bundles over S^2, and suppose a gem-induced trisection of M yields a trisection of the associated closed 4-manifold ̄M with the same central surface, giving the inequality g_T(̄M) ≤ g_GT(M). What conditions on the gem guarantee that this upper bound is sharp, i.e. that g_T(̄M) = g_GT(M)?
accepted.context_brief: Sharpness of the first indirect approach

evidence.quote: On the other hand, it would also be interesting to investigate conditions on the gems of a compact 4-manifold, so that in Theorem 13 the equality holds.

accepted.question_text: Can one algorithmically choose, for a given gem, which 4-colored edges should be used for stabilizations so that the genus of the resulting trisection is as small as possible, thereby producing the best gem-based upper bound for the trisection genus of the associated closed 4-manifold?

evidence.quote: Starting from a given gem (for example, by using its alphanumerical code: see [17]), it is possible to determine algorithmically the best choice of edges to use for stabilizations, so as to minimize the genus of the arising trisection, and hence get a better estimation of the trisection genus of the associated closed 4-manifold.

accepted.question_text: Given a gem, can one automatically test whether the edge-ordering condition (*) of Proposition 11 holds and, when it does, algorithmically extract the specific bicolored cycles that determine a trisection diagram of the associated gem-induced trisection?

evidence.quote: Starting from a given gem, it is obviously possible to check in an automatic way whether condition (*) of Proposition 11 is satisfied; if so, it should not be difficult to detect algorithmically the bicolored cycles yielding a trisection diagram of the associated gem-induced trisection.
